content: 1. It is essential to evaluate whether the services provided are user-friendly. This includes analyzing the referral processes, both incoming and outgoing, to understand who is involved and how these referrals are made. 2. The success of networking, awareness-raising efforts, and referral mechanisms should be assessed to ensure they are effective. 3. Follow-up services must be tracked, including the number of follow-ups conducted and the individuals involved, to confirm that all users receive appropriate follow-up care regardless of their location or the type of service unit they access, whether centralized or decentralized. 4. Repair services should be monitored to determine how often they are required, the types of repairs needed, and the reasons for these repairs. This helps assess the technical quality of the products delivered. 5. The frequency of prosthesis and orthosis replacements should be analyzed to estimate the lifespan of these products and calculate annual production needs. 6. The abandonment rates of prostheses and orthoses, along with the reasons for abandonment, should be studied to identify quality issues and areas for improvement. 7. The primary causes of disability should be determined to identify the main types of treatment required. Monitoring these trends over time can guide service planning and predict future training needs. 8. Data collection and analysis should be integrated into the daily operations of service units. Service user management systems should be fully utilized to extract relevant statistics, preferably in graphical form, to illustrate trends over time. 9. The international prosthetics and orthotics community can support data collection and analysis by developing standardized, user-friendly tools and methods for use at both service and national levels. 10. The confidentiality and privacy of users must be respected by anonymizing data collected for statistical purposes. 11. At the national level, stakeholders require data to monitor service delivery and plan in greater detail. National statistics can be compiled to analyze trends over time and identify areas requiring action to improve service delivery. 12. Information about service delivery should be prepared for decision-makers to raise awareness about the achievements, challenges, and overall role of prosthetics and orthotics services. 13. Data is also valuable for insurance companies, which may be willing to invest in data collection. Standardized tools and methods can facilitate this process. 14. Data compilation at the national level can be streamlined by directly entering data into a national database, such as a register, which could be linked to or integrated into the national health management information system. 15. A national register is essentially a database where service providers submit results to provide a comprehensive view of prosthetics and orthotics services. Regional or provincial registers can supply data to the national register. 16. In countries where there is a risk of users requesting subsidized or free services from multiple providers, a national register of users and services provided can help coordinate efforts and prevent overlap in supply. 17. A national register can also be used to collect data for planning, monitoring, evaluation, and awareness-raising. Licensed service providers should be expected to submit a defined set of data to the responsible national organization. 18. Decisions should be made on how data will be collected, maintained, and retained. An expanded national register could include cross-sectoral data on interventions throughout the continuum of care, such as from amputation to prosthetic fitting and complete rehabilitation. 19. Data collected at the service and national levels is also of interest globally and can be compiled by international stakeholders in prosthetics and orthotics. Global statistics can highlight challenges faced by these services worldwide and provide examples of successful service delivery systems. 20. Standardized evaluation criteria and ISO terminology for prosthetics and orthotics would facilitate international comparisons and exchanges. 21. Users returning for repairs or renewals of their devices can provide feedback on the usefulness, frequency of use, and impact of their prosthesis or orthosis on their ability to work, attend school, participate in social activities, and improve self-determination and confidence. 22. Systematic data collection as part of service delivery is an economical way to assess impact. For more detailed and scientifically accurate assessments, impact studies may be conducted, requiring government or stakeholder commitment and funding. 23. Verifying the impact of services is in the interest of all parties to ensure investments yield good results. Impact studies often involve visiting beneficiaries in their communities to establish a baseline and measure changes over time. 24. Awareness-raising about prosthetics and orthotics is crucial, as these services are often misunderstood or unknown, even within the health sector. Many potential beneficiaries are unaware of their existence, leading to a false impression of low demand. 25. Governments and national stakeholders should promote the use of assistive devices and technologies, making prosthetics and orthotics services known and emphasizing their indispensability. 26. Awareness-raising strategies should be rights-based, referencing national laws and international documents like the CRPD and SDGs, and should also highlight the social and economic benefits of these services. 27. Cultural barriers, such as the perception of disability as a punishment, should be addressed to ensure access to prosthetics and orthotics services for all. 28. User groups play a vital role in lobbying for policies and raising awareness about the need for these services. Their demands complement collected data and help sensitize decision-makers to real experiences. 29. Awareness-raising should be integrated into the training of health and social professionals and supported by referral networks. 30. At the grassroots level, awareness can be raised through collaboration with programs targeting similar groups, such as poverty reduction initiatives, vaccination campaigns, and disability-inclusive sports and recreation programs. 31. The availability of high-quality, accessible, and affordable services directly raises awareness among potential users. Satisfied users often become ambassadors for the prosthetics and orthotics sector. 32. International awareness-raising activities can support national and local initiatives by providing adaptable guidance and information resources. 33. Information campaigns targeting the general public, decision-makers, health professionals, social workers, and potential users should be conducted through various media, including television, radio, newspapers, the Internet, and social media. 34. Good role models, such as visible users in everyday situations or sports events, can help raise awareness and strengthen the image of prosthetics and orthotics services. 35. Sports and recreation programs are important for health and well-being and can benefit prosthetics and orthotics users by promoting physical training and social inclusion. 36. Prosthetics and orthotics service units should collaborate with disability-inclusive sports programs to provide technical support and ensure the provision and maintenance of devices, enabling participation in sports and raising awareness about the rights of people with disabilities. 37. The prosthetics and orthotics profession is often misunderstood as technical or craft work, which undermines its importance. National stakeholders should work to change this perception and highlight the extensive training and theoretical knowledge required for this profession. 38. Prosthetists and orthotists should be recognized as equal to other health and rehabilitation professionals, such as physiotherapists and occupational therapists, and their contributions to the health sector should be emphasized. 39. Measures to strengthen the image of prosthetists and orthotists include integrating their services into hospitals, presenting positive outcomes, promoting national recognition, ensuring professionalism, and maintaining a professional appearance in service units. 40. Prosthetics and orthotics units should be closely linked to orthopedic, surgical, rehabilitation, physiotherapy, and occupational therapy departments to enhance effectiveness and elevate the profession's status. 41. Positive outcomes, such as improved functioning, participation, and socioeconomic gains, should be demonstrated to highlight the value of prosthetics and orthotics services. 42. National recognition of prosthetics and orthotics training, the profession, and the sector should be promoted, including the establishment of national associations or societies. 43. All personnel in prosthetics and orthotics should be well-trained and use evidence-based technologies and methods. 44. Service units should have a professional appearance, with user areas resembling modern hospitals and providing a welcoming, comfortable environment.
